courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Time and the Medieval Cosmos
courses.description: This course introduces first-year students to the basic motions of the solar system as viewed from the Earth along with the mechanical and mathematical models used to reproduce them, while exploring the history of medieval and early modern education, theology, and natural philosophy.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Latin American Revolutions
courses.description: This course explores the problem of revolutionary upheaval in Latin American history, from the revolutionary wars of the independence era (1810-1825) to revolutionary episodes of the 20th century.

source.text: HIST 51. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-PAST or FC-POWER.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Conflicts over Israel/Palestine
courses.description: This course will familiarize students with the background of this ongoing conflict. It will begin with the growth of political Zionism in Europe, continue through early Zionist settlement, the United Nations partition and resulting war, and the history of the conflict through the present.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Traveling to European Cities: American Writers/Cultural Identities, 1830-2000
courses.description: This course examines the experiences of American writers who traveled and lived in European cities during the era between 1830 and 1930 with the goal of developing historical insights into these writers' fascination with famous European cities and the experience of travel.

source.text: HIST 53. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-PAST.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Movies and the Medieval Past
courses.description: Movies set in the past can have a compelling and sometimes misleading influence on how people visualize and understand history. In this seminar, we will analyze a number of movies set in the era of the Middle Ages, considering their merits and drawbacks not only as entertainment, but as a form of historical memory.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Preventing Broken Hearts in North Carolina: History and Health Care in the South
courses.description: How do scientists and humanists approach complex problems and work together to solve them? Team-taught by a doctor and a historian, this class explores how our state's health care system changed over the last fifty years, how those changes have affected people, and how history shapes both doctors and patients.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Movies and the Medieval Past
courses.description: In this class, students explore representations of the European Middle Ages in modern films, examining how cinema has represented and distorted memories of the medieval era. Students will also consider how such cinematic visions of the medieval world might reflect the politics, culture, and social values that characterized the period of the film's production.

source.text: HIST 56. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-PAST.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Dogs, Past and Present
courses.description: As workers and companions, dogs have shared human history from its origins. Human society constitutes their natural habitat. Understanding dogs therefore requires analyzing their relationships to and meaning for people: What problems result from the daily close proximity of people and dogs--and how have societies coped with them? How and why have people projected onto dogs their assumptions about humanity? How have the answers to these questions changed as human societies have changed?

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: History and the Meaning of Life
courses.description: How do we find meaning in our lives? How should we think about our families, ambitions, and fears? How do individual lives fit into the grand sweep of human history? In this seminar, students will learn to read deeply and apply the tools of historical analysis in order to tackle the biggest possible questions.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Rebuilding the American South: Work and Identity in Modern History
courses.description: This course examines how class experiences and debates over the meaning of work have shaped the postbellum Southern United States. Students will analyze how the South's technological innovation, politics, urban planning, consumer economy, and social movements have impacted the racial, gender, and sexual identities of its people.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Nations, Borders, and Identities
courses.description: This seminar will explore the ways people have identified themselves in relation to specific places, nation-states, and foreign "others." Examples may include the Kurdish nationalists, Islamist political parties, the Eritrean independence movement, and the Basque separatists.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Water, Conflict, and Connection: the Middle East and Ottoman Lands
courses.description: Water has played pivotal roles in the histories, societies, and politics of Middle Eastern peoples. This course will survey the role of water in religious and cultural practices, technological innovations that facilitate agriculture, public health issues arising from water-borne diseases, and the contribution of water scarcity to cross-border political conflicts. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Gorbachev: The Collapse of the Soviet Empire and the Rise of the New Russia
courses.description: Examines Mikhail Gorbachev and the astonishing transformations that occurred while he governed the Soviet Union between 1985 and 1991. Students will explore post-Soviet Russia's efforts at negotiating a new set of relations with the rest of the world and how Russia continues to shape our own destiny.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Film and History in Europe and the United States, 1908-1968
courses.description: This course will examine major films in Europe and America from 1908 to 1968 in terms of how they shaped the medium and reflected important social trends.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Maid in America, Made in China: Laboring Women in Global Perspective
courses.description: Public figures ranging from former U.S. President Jimmy Carter to New York Times columnist Nicholas Kristof have suggested women's increased entry into the labor market as a cure for the problems that face their families and their societies. But scholars have demonstrated that paid work has offered women new freedoms while subjecting them to new forms of control. This course will explore that paradox by examining women's diverse experiences as workers historically and today.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Seeing History in Everyday Places: Chapel Hill as a Case Study
courses.description: Our homes, our workplaces, our towns, our natural areas-all are products of history, shaped by people, rich with meaning and full of surprises. Using Chapel Hill as our living laboratory, we will explore new ways of understanding the past and how it shapes the world we live in now.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Global Food History
courses.description: What does it mean to study food history, and how do we approach it from a global perspective? The world of food (and the food of the world) is a huge subject, and the focus in this class will be on historical texts and topics (as opposed to contemporary food issues), and on global examples (with an emphasis on non-Western regions, particularly Asia). Class topics will center on three major themes: Food as Nation; Food as Gender; Food as Systems.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Women's Voices: 20th-Century European History in Female Memory
courses.description: The course examines 20th-century European history through the lenses of women's autobiographical writings. It explores women's voices from different generational, social, and national backgrounds and asks what formed their memories. Honors version available.

source.text: HIST 72. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-PAST or FC-POWER.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Emperors, Courts, and Consumption: The Mughals of India
courses.description: Through a study of autobiographical texts, contemporary accounts, objects, architecture and later representations in scholarly works, films and novels, we will undertake a thematic investigation of the Mughal Empire (1526-1858), focusing on the period of the first six Mughal rulers of India.

source.text: HIST 74. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Understanding 1492
courses.description: This seminar will examine one of the most challenging topics in American and Latin American history: how to understand the conquest (la conquista) of Latin America by the Spaniards after the arrival of Columbus after 1492.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: United States and the Caribbean
courses.description: This seminar provides a thematic examination of US-Caribbean relations spanning the ''Spanish-American War'' in the late nineteenth century to US-Central America relations - with attention to the ''root causes'' of Central American migration to the United States - in the early twenty-first century. Students will study US-Caribbean relations as a process within the logic of competing national interests and conflicting national aspirations.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Coming of Age in 20th Century America
courses.description: We will employ coming of age autobiographies to explore developments in the US during the 20th century. In these autobiographies the authors focus primarily on the periods of childhood and adolescence into young adulthood. We will consider many issues including: race, racism, immigration, religion, social class, and gender.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: African American Music as History
courses.description: This course uses music to explore African-American life in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Students will investigate how African Americans, across time and space and in search of opportunity, created, used and marketed music. The course will examine three core groups-artists, music entrepreneurs and audiences.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Diaries, Memoirs, and Testimonies of the Holocaust
courses.description: In ghettos and hiding places during the Holocaust, European Jews and other victims of Nazism recorded their experiences in diaries and other chronicles. Students will read diaries and memoirs as well as listen to testimonies to understand Holocaust history through life narratives, exploring tensions between history and memory.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: African History through Popular Music
courses.description: Examines popular music as a way of understanding African history from the 1930s to the present. We will read background materials on African historical developments and musical styles, do a lot of listening, and try to learn what African musicians tell us about their societies.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Monsters, Murders, and Mayhem in Microhistorical Analysis: French Case Studies
courses.description: Explores the distinctive features of microhistorical approaches to the past and the attractions of microhistory for the practicing historian. Students will read a rich sampling of recent work (much of it featuring monsters, murder, and mayhem) and try their hand at writing their own microhistories. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: What Concentration Camp Survivors Tell Us
courses.description: This is a seminar about reading so as to learn as much as we can from individuals expressing the inexpressible. It asks what (if anything) only camp survivors can tell us about the experience and what we can learn by exploring the effects of this experience on survivors. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Witchcraft and Magic in the Early Modern Atlantic World
courses.description: This seminar explores early modern witchcraft and magic to introduce students to the ways in which historians think about questions of gender, power, and belief in historical perspective. The seminar will focus on how historians pose problems, collect evidence, and evaluate knowledge about how witchcraft and magic reveal broader tensions in the early modern world.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: The Environment in American History
courses.description: In this course, students will analyze the ways in which Americans have both shaped and been shaped by their natural environment. Together, we will trace a selected history of interactions between humans and nature in America, focusing on the often-fraught intersection between political, economic, social, and religious understandings of nature. This is a dynamic course that requires students to connect the lessons of history to the world they inhabit today by engaging with popular journalism, literature, podcasts, and more, and through class visits around campus to explore how the environmental history we study has shaped even their most immediate surroundings.

source.text: HIST 87. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-PAST, COMMBEYOND.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First Year Seminar: America's Founding Documents
courses.description: This first-year seminar introduces students to the foundations of U.S. democracy through its most significant speeches, declarations, letters, proclamations, and other writings. We will identify and analyze the political, historical, and cultural impact of founding documents on governance and democracy in America, identify and analyze the political, historical, and cultural impact of key milestones in American history on the evolution of democratic republicanism, evaluate key concepts, principles, arguments and contexts in founding documents of the American republic, and evaluate key milestones in progress and challenges in the effort to form ''a more perfect Union.''

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: First Year Seminar: Special Topics
courses.description: Special topics course. Content will vary each semester. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: A History of Lies, Conspiracies, and Misinformation
courses.description: This course, geared towards undergraduate students at the beginning of their college careers, will give students the tools needed to critically evaluate information. Texts from different historical periods, newsreels and propaganda movies, and a variety of different websites will be examined and deconstructed to understand how content can be presented or manipulated.

source.text: HIST 101. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-PAST, FAD.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Introduction to Major Problems in U.S History
courses.description: This course explores major events and trends in U.S. history from the pre-colonial period to the 21st century. It offers students an introduction to some of the most important developments in the nation's past and the tools to understand them. We will examine the evolution of political participation and discourse, fundamental changes and continuities in economic life, and the rise and fall of numerous social movements.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Introduction to Major Problems in Modern World History
courses.description: This survey course explores major events and trends in global history from 1200 to the present. We will examine societies across six continents while focusing on several key themes and developments, including social and economic diversity and transformation; exchange, conflict, and evolution within and between societies; the rise and fall of imperial projects; and the parameters and consequences of global interconnectedness across time.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Introduction to Major Problems in European History
courses.description: This course explores major events and themes in European history from the Early Modern period through the present. We will focus our attention on several key religious, social, and political developments, including the growth of the modern state and economy, the history and legacy of European imperialism, the rise and fall of various intellectual and social movements and their effects on society, and the making and unmaking of identities based on culture, nation, and region.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Empires in World History
courses.description: This course explores and compares premodern and/or modern empires on a global scale, inquiring into rulers' strategies and subject peoples' experiences. Empires studied will depend on instructor's area of expertise, but may include Greeks, Romans, Chinese, Incas, West Africans, Mughals, and Ottomans, among others. Previously offered as HIST 345 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Ancient History
courses.description: A topical survey of the ancient world, especially the civilization of the Near East, Greece, and Rome.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Medieval History
courses.description: A survey of Western Europe and the Mediterranean World, 300-1500.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Introduction to Early Medieval History 500-1050
courses.description: An introductory-level survey of early medieval political, cultural, religious and social history between ca.500 and ca.1050 with a geographical focus on Europe. This course also considers eastern Christianity and Islam, as well as parts of Asia, for comparison. Throughout the course students will closely analyze the evidence for the period.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Introduction to the Cultures and Histories of Native North America
courses.description: An interdisciplinary introduction to Native American history and studies. The course uses history, literature, art, and cultural studies to study the Native American experience.

source.text: HIST 110. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | AMST 110 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Global Food History
courses.description: This course is designed to be a thematic introduction to the study of global food history, from ancient times to the present, with particular emphasis on the food-ways of non-Western regions, such as Afro-Caribbean, Chinese, Indian, Japanese, and Mexican.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Sport and American History
courses.description: A survey of American sport history, from the colonial era to the present. Course will explore how sports have reflected larger trends in American life and analyze the different ways sports have influenced American history and shaped the world we occupy today.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of Religion in North America
courses.description: Surveys religious thought and practice in the United States and Canada from the colonial era to the present day. Themes include continuities and changes in expressing ancient faiths; the relationship between religion and politics; the intersection of theology with everyday life; and evolving notions of religious truth and toleration.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: United States History through Film
courses.description: Explores the history of the United States through films made about various historical eras. For each film, the instructor will lecture on the time period(s), the class will read relevant primary and secondary sources, and then the class will watch and discuss the film.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Social History of Popular Music in 20th-Century America
courses.description: Explores the relationship between popular music and major developments in 20th-century America. The course's overarching focus is how popular music has simultaneously unified and divided the nation.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Early American History and the Foundations of American Democracy
courses.description: A survey of various aspects of American development during the colonial, revolutionary, and national periods, with stress upon the foundations of American democracy. Students may not receive credit for both HIST 126 and HIST 127 .

source.text: HIST 126. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER, FAD.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: American History to 1865
courses.description: A survey of various aspects of American development during the colonial, revolutionary, and national periods, with stress upon major themes and interpretations. Students may not receive credit for both HIST 126 and HIST 127 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: American History since 1865
courses.description: A survey of various aspects of American development during a century of rapid industrial, social, political, and international change, with stress upon major themes and interpretations.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Very Modern America, 1985-2025
courses.description: This course explores the history of the United States in the very recent past. Through a sustained analysis of key political, cultural, economic, and social developments, students will gain a deeper understanding of the complex issues and problems that shape American life today.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern African History
courses.description: An overview of major developments in sub-Saharan African history since the late 19th century, focusing on colonialism, nationalism and decolonization, social change, and current issues, and drawing upon fiction, film, and primary sources.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Southeast Asia before 1800 through Digital History
courses.description: This course will cover the history of the territories and peoples of Southeast Asia (comprising the modern-day countries of Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand, Timor-Leste, Singapore and Vietnam), from earliest times to 1800. The course will also delve into debates about the past, who is engaged in such debates, and how to navigate these debates to find reliable historical sources and communicate analysis of those sources for a wide audience.

source.text: HIST 131. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | ASIA 131 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern Southeast Asia
courses.description: The history of Southeast Asia from the 19th century to the present. Long-term political, economic, social, and intellectual questions, including the impact of imperialism, the rise of nationalism, the transformation of the economy, the Cold War, and the coherence of Southeast Asia as a region.

source.text: HIST 132. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | ASIA 132 , PWAD 132 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Introduction to Chinese History
courses.description: Chinese history from its beginnings to the present, organized around the central theme of how the identity of China and 'Chineseness' was created.

source.text: HIST 133. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | ASIA 133 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern East Asia
courses.description: Comparative and interdisciplinary introduction to China, Korea, and Japan in the 19th and 20th centuries, focusing on impact of the West, nation building, industrialization, and evolution of mass society.

source.text: HIST 134. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | ASIA 134 , PWAD 134 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of the Indian Subcontinent to 1750
courses.description: An introduction to major political, religious, social, and cultural events from 3500 BCE to 1750 CE with a focus on Hindu, Muslim, and Buddhist groups before British colonial rule.

source.text: HIST 135. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-PAST. | ASIA 135 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh: South Asia since 1750
courses.description: This course is an introduction to modern India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. We will investigate major political, social, economic, and cultural issues from 1750 to the present.

source.text: HIST 136. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | ASIA 136 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Muhammad to Malcolm X: Islam, Politics, Race, and Gender
courses.description: This course provides an introduction to the history of the Islamic world from the time of the Prophet Muhammad to the present day. It seeks to expose students to key themes, individuals, and movements that have represented Islamic thought and practice, and enable students to engage directly with intra-Islamic debates.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of Muslim Societies to 1500
courses.description: A broad, comprehensive, and interdisciplinary introduction to the traditional civilization of the Muslim world. Students may not receive credit for both HIST 138 / ASIA 138 and ASIA 180 / RELI 180 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of Muslim Societies since 1500
courses.description: A broad interdisciplinary survey of the later Islamic empires since the 15th century and their successor societies in the modern Muslim world. Students may not receive credit for both ASIA 139 / HIST 139 and ASIA 181 / RELI 181 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The World since 1945
courses.description: This introduction to the contemporary world examines the Cold War and its international aftermath, decolonization, national development across a variety of cases, and trends in the global economy.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Globalization Since 1500
courses.description: Course explores how commodities have connected people and places around the world since 1500. Lectures, readings, and recitations focus on tracing the histories of specific commodities (e.g., sugar, opium, and uranium) across different contexts. Significant sub-themes include the history of business, international human rights, and science and technology.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Latin America under Colonial Rule
courses.description: Social and economic development under colonial rule, especially in Mexico and Peru.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Latin America since Independence
courses.description: A general introduction to Latin American society, culture, politics, and economics from a historical perspective. Focus will be on the events of the past two centuries.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Women in United States History
courses.description: This course will survey the history of women, gender relations, and notions of sex difference in the United States from the colonial era to present times, with a special emphasis on women's varied experiences and expectations across divisions of class, race, and region. Key themes will include work, politics, citizenship, reproduction, sociability, and sexuality.

source.text: HIST 144. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | WGST 144 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Latin American Indigenous Peoples
courses.description: This course surveys the history of Latin American indigenous peoples from the conquest to the present. Focus is on indigenous struggles and survival strategies. Previously offered as HIST 527.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: European History to 1650
courses.description: European history from Greek antiquity to the mid-17th century.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: European History since 1650
courses.description: European history from the middle of the 17th century to the present.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: From the Bible to Broadway: Jewish History to Modern Times
courses.description: This class surveys the history of the Jews from ancient to modern times. It focuses on the development of Jewish religion, culture identity, and politics in Jewish communities in the Western, Atlantic and Middle Eastern Worlds. It also explores the development of antisemitism and anti-Jewish violence.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The British Empire, 1815-1994
courses.description: This course explores the modern empire from slavery and abolition, through Independence and the Cold War. Focusing on parts of Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, and the British Isles, we will consider issues of race, gender, religion, wealth inequality, war, and anti-colonialism. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Early Modern European History, 1450-1815
courses.description: Intellectual and social structures, dynamics of social and political change, principles of authority, and bases of revolution from the Reformation to the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic period.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Europe and the World Since 1900
courses.description: An overview of modern European history from the First World War to the present, covering major themes such as imperialism and decolonization; competing political ideologies; "hot" and "cold" wars; the Holocaust and Holocaust memory; gender and sexuality; migration and labor; race and religion; the European Union; local community-building; and efforts to redefine Europe and its place in the wider world.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Russia Becomes an Empire
courses.description: Between 862 and 1861 Russia expanded from agrarian settlements into Europe's most formidable empire. Subjugated by Mongols in 1240, it recovered and absorbed territories from Poland to Alaska. Conquest came on the backs of an enserfed peasantry, whose emancipation began the next chapter in Russia's history.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Russia under the Last Tsars and Soviet Commissars
courses.description: This course surveys fundamental issues affecting the Russian/Soviet/post-Soviet multinational empire in the last century and a half, emphasizing regime failures, revolutions, wars, and ethnic challenges.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern Central Asia
courses.description: This course offers an introduction to the political, religious, cultural, and social history of ''Russia'' Central Asia (which you may have heard of as ''the five 'stans'') from the eighteenth century to the present day. We will conceptualize the Eurasian space across modern political boundaries by charting the evolution of several themes in different parts of the region. These themes include Islam, the state, ideology, gender, and the environment. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Victorian Britain: From Slavery to South African War
courses.description: This course explores political, social, and cultural history from the Napoleonic Wars through the South African War. Surveys the history of the United Kingdom in the context of Britain's imperial expansion, including slavery, reform, women's suffrage, social movements, and Victorian wealth and poverty.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: 20th Century Britain: from the Great War to Brexit
courses.description: This course explores political, social, and cultural history from 1900 to the present: the two world wars, the declining empire, the extension of parliamentary democracy, the new welfare state, and a deeply diverse racial, ethnic, and religious society where social and economic differences remain. Who is British?

source.text: HIST 165. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-PAST. | EURO 165 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of Afghanistan
courses.description: The American occupation of Afghanistan after 9/11/2001, the longest war in United States history, continues a long pattern of great empires attempting to control the country. This course asks why it has been challenging for Afghanistan's rulers, both foreign and domestic, to build a centralized state in an historically decentralized society.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Asian American History
courses.description: This course examines the history of Asian Americans, focusing on how key events, conflicts, and continuities have shaped their experiences within the broader American context. By engaging with primary sources, such as historical documents and personal narratives, students will learn to evaluate, synthesize, and communicate evidence about the human past. This course encourages students to apply historical insights to contemporary issues, fostering an understanding of how the material and historical past influences our perception of both the past and present.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Honors Seminar in African, Asian, and Middle Eastern History
courses.description: Examines selected themes in the history of Africa, Asia, and/or the Middle East. Theme(s) chosen by the instructor. Possible subjects: colonialism, resistance movements, religion, gender, economic transformations.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Honors Seminar in Latin American History
courses.description: Examines selected themes in the history of Latin America. Theme(s) chosen by the instructor. Possible subjects: indigenous societies, colonialism, religion, the family, economic transformations.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Honors Seminar in Russian, Eurasian, and Eastern European History
courses.description: Examines selected themes in the history of Russia, Eurasia, and/or Eastern Europe. Theme(s) chosen by the instructor. Possible subjects: imperialism, revolution, the Soviet Union, war and society.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Honors Seminar in Early European History
courses.description: Examines selected themes in the history of Europe from ancient to early modern times. Theme(s) chosen by the instructor. Possible subjects: legacies of antiquity, philosophy and religion, feudal society, gender, and power.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Honors Seminar in Modern European History
courses.description: Examines selected themes in the history of modern Europe. Theme(s) chosen by the instructor. Possible subjects: effects of industrialism, nationalism, history of ideas, consumer society, modern revolutions, imperialism.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Honors Seminar in American History
courses.description: Examines selected themes in American history. Theme(s) chosen by the instructor. Possible subjects: colonial diversity, emerging nation, intellectual traditions, labor and capitalism, slavery and race relations, markets and political power, war and society.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Global World Order from World War II to the Present
courses.description: This course deals with the establishment of the rules-based global order toward the end of the Second World War and analyzes the development of that order throughout the Cold War years and the post-Cold War era up to the present. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Special Topics in History
courses.description: Subject matter will vary with instructor but will focus on some particular topic or historical approach. Course description available from the departmental office. Closed to graduate students.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit. 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Special Topics in History, FC-PAST
courses.description: Subject matter will vary with instructor but will focus on some particular topic or historical approach.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Empires and Cultures in the Modern World
courses.description: This course will examine the relationship between Asia, Africa, the Middle East, Latin America, and the making of the modern world in the 20th century.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Global Environmental Histories: People, Climate, and Landscapes
courses.description: Global warming? Hurricanes, floods, fires, food security: focusing on critical issues of human rights and changing forces in our natural world, this course prepares students to explore different sources on a variety of topics for present-day environmental issues and the entangled relations between nature and society on our planet.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: War, Diplomacy, and Statecraft, 1618-1815
courses.description: The history of European international politics from the outbreak of the Thirty Years War to the Congress of Vienna. Considers the sources of national power, the reasons for war, and the changing nature of diplomacy.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: War, Diplomacy, and Statecraft, 1815-1945
courses.description: The history of international politics from the fall of Napoleon to the end of the Second World War, with special attention to European nationalism, imperialism, the emergence of non-European great powers, the reasons for war, and the search for peace.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Global Cold War
courses.description: A survey of the Cold War from its origins in the aftermath of the Second World War to its conclusion in the late 1980s. Focuses on the geopolitical, military, ideological, and economic aspects of the global superpower conflict.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Genocide in Global Perspective
courses.description: The class begins with colonial contexts before moving to the late Ottoman Empire. After consideration of genocides in Europe in the first half of the twentieth century, the focus shifts to the violence of decolonization and postcolonial conflict. The class also asks whether genocide is a useful category of analysis. Previously offered as HIST 180.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Global Issues and Globalization
courses.description: Survey of international social, political, and cultural patterns in selected societies of Africa, Asia, America, and Europe, stressing comparative analysis of conflicts and change in different historical contexts. LAC recitation sections offered in French, German, and Spanish.

source.text: HIST 210I. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-POWER, INTERDISCI. | GLBL 210I , ANTH 210I , GEOG 210I , POLI 210I .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: God and Government in America
courses.description: A survey of the relationship between religion, government, and political culture in the U.S. and Canada from the colonial era to the present.

source.text: HIST 211. | 3 Credits. | FC-CREATE or FC-PAST, FAD.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of Sea Power
courses.description: The influence of sea power on international affairs will be surveyed from ancient times to the present. Emphasis on United States naval history and its interaction with diplomacy, economics, and technology.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Air Power and Modern Warfare
courses.description: Examines air power theory and practice from 1914 to the present. Focuses on the application of air power as an instrument of war and the effectiveness of that application.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Peoples, Cultures, and Landscapes of Latin America
courses.description: Peoples, Cultures, and Landscapes of Latin America explores the peopling of the Americas by Amerindian, African and Afro descendant peoples, and Europeans. It will consider the inequalities of power, wealth, and autonomy across gender, ethnicity, and class in Latin America to understand more fully their deep historical roots and their persistence into our own time. We will learn how Latin America takes on greater meaning, when we consider this subcontinent in different phases of globalization.

source.text: HIST 215. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | LTAM 215 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of Mapping: From Sea Monsters to Google Earth
courses.description: This course examines the history of maps and mapmaking as a way to understand how societies have defined, interpreted, and represented geographic knowledge over time. We will focus especially on early modern cartography and the Age of Discovery, while also examining how contemporary technologies like Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Google Earth continue these traditions of spatial representation.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Asian American Studies
courses.description: This interdisciplinary examination of 'Asian America' takes a rigorous approach via both primary and secondary texts to study the different groups most often identified as Asian American, their histories, legalities, sociology, and culture, and how they have developed within and in relation to the United States.

source.text: HIST 217I. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER, INTERDISCI. | ENGL 217I , AMST 217I .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Olympic Games: A Global History
courses.description: Course uses the history of the modern Olympic Games (1896-present) to explore both global sport and the history of international relations. Topics include sport and the Cold War; terrorism; human rights; the anti-apartheid movement; and issues of race, class, gender, disability; and the question of who is a "real" athlete. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Under Crescent and Cross: Jews in the Medieval World
courses.description: This course examines the history of Jewish communities in the medieval world. Particular attention will focus on relations between Jews, Muslims, and Christians in diverse historical contexts--from the Indian Ocean and the Middle East to the Mediterranean and western Europe.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of Greece
courses.description: A survey of Greek history and culture from the Bronze Age to the Hellenistic period.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Rise of Rome
courses.description: Origins to the first two centuries CE. Focuses upon Rome's growth as a world power and the shift from republican government to autocracy.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Fall of the Roman Empire
courses.description: The decline and transformation of the Roman Empire, from its apogee in the second century until the rise of Islam in the seventh century. Covers topics like the Christianization of Rome, the barbarian invasions, the role of climate and pandemic disease, and the end of the ancient Mediterranean world system.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Medieval Science
courses.description: This course explores forms of scientific thinking before the modern era, focusing mainly on the intellectual tradition in medieval Europe ca. 500-1500. Special attention will be devoted to the intersections of scientific concepts and Christian religious ideas.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The History of London 43 - 1666
courses.description: This course traces the first three-quarters of London's rich two-thousand-year history, from the Romans to the Great Fire. Students examine how London evolved as an urban environment. They also study London's many and varied relationships with the wider world, including, in the latter part of the course, North America. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Native American History: The East
courses.description: Covers the histories of American Indians east of the Mississippi River and before 1840. The approach is ethnohistorical.

source.text: HIST 231. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-PAST. | AMST 231 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: American Indian and Indigenous History: The West
courses.description: This course is designed to introduce students to the histories of American Indians living west of the Mississippi. We will examine the historical processes and issues that have shaped the lives of Indigenous Americans over the past five centuries from creation stories to the late 20th century. Given the expansive chronology we will examine the broad themes of each era while spending time diving into the histories and cultures of a select few Indigenous communities.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Native American Tribal Studies
courses.description: This course introduces students to a tribally specific body of knowledge. The tribal focus of the course and the instructor change from term to term. Honors version available.

source.text: HIST 234. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-PAST. | AMST 234 , ANTH 234 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Native America in the 20th Century
courses.description: This course deals with the political, economic, social, and cultural issues important to 20th-century Native Americans as they attempt to preserve tribalism in the modern world.

source.text: HIST 235. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | AMST 235 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Sex and American History
courses.description: Does sex have a history? This course argues that it does. Exploring American history from the earliest encounters of Indians, Europeans, and Africans through the aftermath of the sexual revolution, we will consider diverse perspectives, important dynamics of change, and surprising ways in which the past informs our present--and our selves.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Colonial American History to 1763
courses.description: An in-depth history of colonial North America. Topics include: interactions among Native Americans, Europeans, and Africans and the founding and development of English, French, and Spanish colonies in the lands that eventually became the United States.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The American Revolution, 1763-1815
courses.description: An in-depth history of the American Revolution. Topics include: causes of the split between Britain and 13 of its colonies, the fighting of the Revolutionary War, and the creation of the United States.

source.text: HIST 238. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER, FAD. | PWAD 238 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Religion in North America since 1865
courses.description: A survey of modern religion in the United States and Canada. Themes include religious pluralism; new religious movements, immigrant faiths; the relationship between religion and urban life, industrialization, and new science; religion and foreign affairs; questions of church and state; and the conflict between secular modernity and religious fundamentalism.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Introduction to Mexico: A Nation in Four Revolutions
courses.description: History of Mexico seen through four moments of change: conquest, independence, 19th-century reforms, and 20th-century revolution. This course is an introductory survey for students who want to know more about Mexico, its place in Latin America, and its relations with the United States.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of Latinos in the United States
courses.description: A comparative examination of the historical experiences of Latinos in the United States, from the 19th century to the present, drawing on experiences of Mexican Americans, Puerto Ricans, Dominicans, and Central Americans. Special emphasis on the events, people, and ideas that have made distinctive contributions.

source.text: HIST 241. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | LTAM 241 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: United States-Latin American Relations
courses.description: This course examines the history of United States involvement in Latin America and the Caribbean. Lectures will cover two centuries of United States intervention, from the wars of the 19th century to the covert CIA operations of the Cold War and the more recent wars on drugs and terror.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The United States and Africa
courses.description: This course traces changing relationships between the United States and sub-Saharan Africa from the 17th century to the present. Topics include the trans-Atlantic slave trade, back-to-Africa movements and the colonization of Liberia by African Americans, United States policies toward decolonizing and postcolonial African countries, and contemporary links between Africa and America. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of the American Presidency
courses.description: This course examines the historical evolution of the United States presidency and its role in government and society. The class is especially concerned with the ways that the office and its occupants have been shaped by the aspirations of the American people and the global challenges of the modern era.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The United States and the Cold War: Origins, Development, Legacy
courses.description: This is both a wide-ranging and detailed course that looks at the origins, the evolution, and the termination of the Cold War from 1945 to 1989/90. It also considers the "New Cold War" with Russia that developed in 2014. The course is based on an international and multinational perspective.

source.text: HIST 245. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | PWAD 245 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Great Power Conflicts - the US, Germany/EU, Russia, China: from Hitler & the Cold War to the Present
courses.description: This course considers global politics from World War II to the present. It covers many events, wars & peace deals you always wanted to learn more about. We begin with Hitler's aggressive wars and explore the great power rivalries of the Cold War. We also explore the geopolitical conflicts from the 1990s, including NATO expansion, to the present. We consider US-Europe-Russia-China relations. We analyze the wars in the former Yugoslavia, the Afghanistan and Iraq wars, the never-ending turmoil in the Middle East, and the Taiwan and Indo-Pacific questions as well as many other global security, economic, trade and energy issues.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Early Modern Japanese History and Culture
courses.description: From the 1603 establishment of the Tokugawa Shogunate to the Meiji Restoration of 1868, Japan was ruled by the Tokugawa family in an unusual early modern federation, with a balance of power between the warrior government in Edo and the domanial governments spread across the archipelago. This resemblance of this system to the U.S. balance between federal and state power frames our examination of the early modern period.

source.text: HIST 247. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | JAPN 246 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Guerrillas and Counterinsurgencies in Latin America
courses.description: This course examines the leftist guerrilla movements that swept Latin America and the Caribbean during the latter half of the 20th century. Students will analyze the origins, trajectories, and legacies of these insurgencies, paying particular attention to the roles of race, class, and gender. Previously offered as HIST/PWAD 528.

source.text: HIST 248. | 3 Credits. | FC-CREATE or FC-POWER. | PWAD 248 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern Global Christianity
courses.description: An intermediate survey of global Christianity from the late Middle Ages to the present day that traces evolving theology and worship; the role of religion in the politics of empire; modern challenges to traditional religion; and the international expansion of the faith.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Central Europe, Medieval to Modern
courses.description: This course provides an introduction to the long history of Central Europe before the modern era. This region--between the Baltic and the Alps and between the Rhine and the Bug--was inhabited by a variety of people speaking Germanic, Slavic, Baltic, and Magyar languages. Moving swiftly through the chronology of major events that continually transformed the political landscape of these territories, we ask: how did premodern legacies shape the modern history of Central Europe?

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Thirty Years War (1618-1648): Europe in an Age of Crisis
courses.description: A critical examination of the significance of the Thirty Years' War for 17th-century Europe's social, religious, military, and geopolitical history. The representation of the conflict in art and literature also receives attention.

source.text: HIST 251. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | PWAD 251 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Politics, Society, and Culture in Modern Germany (1871-1945)
courses.description: This course explores the history of Modern Germany, by focusing on Imperial Germany, the Weimar Republic and the Third Reich. We will study continuities and changes in politics, society, and culture and examine the lasting impact of World War I, World War II and the Holocaust.

source.text: HIST 252. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | EURO 252 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: War and Society in Early Modern Europe
courses.description: A critical examination, from the Renaissance to the Napoleonic period, of the changes in European land and naval warfare and their impact on society and government.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Manor to Machine: The Economic Shaping of Europe
courses.description: From agriculture to industry, Europe's march to industrialization. Survey from the medieval manor through revival of trade, rise of towns, credit and capitalism, overseas expansion and mercantilism to the Industrial Revolution.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: France, 1940 to the Present
courses.description: Three events shaped contemporary France: collaboration and resistance in occupied France; the Algerian War; and the political, cultural, and social movements in the late 1960s and 1970s. This class will examine these events, how they are remembered and given meaning, and their role in making the France we know today. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Politics, Society, and Culture in Postwar Germany
courses.description: The interdisciplinary seminar will explore cultural, historical, and political issues of contemporary Germany and analyze German developments from the postwar period to the present. Readings and discussions in English.

source.text: HIST 257. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | POLI 257 , EURO 257 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern Italy since 1848
courses.description: This course focuses on the history of modern Italy and examines changes in political, social, economic structures. Students will engage in the search for an "Italian identity." Topics will include unification, World War I and II, Italian fascism, the postwar Italian Republic, the Mafia, terrorism, popular culture, and Silvio Berlusconi.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Towards Emancipation? Women in Modern Europe
courses.description: This course examines and compares the situation of women in politics, the work force, society and family from the French Revolution to the new women's movement in the 1970s with a focus on Britain, France and Germany. One major theme is the history of the struggle for women's emancipation.

source.text: HIST 259. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | WGST 259 , EURO 259 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: From Kings to Communists: East-Central Europe in the Modern Era
courses.description: A study in the emergence of nations of Eastern Europe, their internal development, mutual conflicts, and struggle for independence. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: France, 1870-1940
courses.description: Third Republic France was riven with conflict. This course examines these conflicts, how the men and women of France and its colonies gave them meaning, and how we in turn can interpret these struggles to develop our understanding of the longest-lived republic in French history (1870-1940).

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of the Holocaust: The Destruction of the European Jews
courses.description: Anti-Semitism; the Jews of Europe; the Hitler dictatorship; evolution of Nazi Jewish policy from persecution to the Final Solution; Jewish response; collaborators, bystanders, and rescuers; aftermath.

source.text: HIST 262. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | JWST 262 , PWAD 262 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Gender and Religion in Premodern Europe
courses.description: This course examines gender in the religious lives of premodern Europeans from 500-1700, both in daily life (marriage, sexuality, devotions) and among the religious elite (clergy, monks and nuns, mystics). Feminist history, masculinity studies, and sexuality studies will all be taught as historical methods, paired with primary source documents from medieval Christians. Honors version available.

source.text: HIST 263. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | RELI 263 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Gender in Russian History
courses.description: Traces the development of sexual identities and changes in masculine and feminine ideals from Tsarist Russia through the post-Soviet period with emphasis on politics, society, and popular culture.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Imperial China in Global Objects
courses.description: This course explores the culture and society of imperial China (pre-1912) through objects. Six kinds of objects - silk, wooden beams and brackets, precious stones, ships and stirrups, silver, and tea - will each form a module that introduces students first to key historical activities associated with the object and then to the diverse sociocultural, economic, and political spheres that they played important roles in.

source.text: HIST 265. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | CHIN 265 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Global History of Warfare
courses.description: The history of warfare from its prehistoric origins to the present. The focus is on interactions between peoples around the world and particularly on the problems of innovation and adaptation. Previously offered as HIST/PWAD 351.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Chinese American History
courses.description: This course approaches Chinese migration to the United States as both a historical subject and a methodological challenge. Rather than limiting this history to events and communities only within the borders of the United States, we ask how law, geopolitics, and gendered experiences shaped the transpacific Chinese communities. At the same time, we take up the questions: How do we know what we know about the past? and How can we read against the bias of the archive to recover marginalized voices? Students will work with diplomatic records, petitions, letters, personal essays, memoirs to grapple with these problems of evidence.

source.text: HIST 267. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | AMST 267 , ASIA 268 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern London: Empire, Race, and Culture
courses.description: Explores the history, culture, and politics of London from the decade before the First World War, through the "Swinging" 1960s, to the recent Olympics fever. Surveys the architecture, cultural institutions and the arts, against the background of the city's changing racial, ethnic, religious, and socio-economic composition. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Mughal India
courses.description: In this course we will investigate one of the most well-known of South Asian polities, and the grandest and longest lasting empire in Indian history, the Mughal Empire (1526-1858), whose rulers and elites were responsible for much of the iconic architecture and painting associated with India today.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Ancient and Medieval Japanese History and Culture
courses.description: This course surveys Japanese history and cultural development from the prehistoric period, rich with archaeological evidence, to the reunification of Japan in the late sixteenth century. One major topic is the mythology or and historical evidence for early state formation, including the role that Japan's long "unbroken" history plays in modern debates about national identity, xenophobia, and relations with regional neighbors. Another focus is the emergence of women's literature.

source.text: HIST 271. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | JAPN 231 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern South Asia
courses.description: Provides students with a critical understanding of the political, economic, and social dynamics of contemporary South Asia. Themes explored include the development (or lack of) democratic structures, continuing relevance of caste and religion, emergence of right wing movements, contesting representations of the past, and the prospects and challenges confronting the region.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Water, Conflict, and Connection in the Middle East
courses.description: Water has played many pivotal roles in the societies and politics of Middle Eastern peoples. This course will survey the history of water in the region, including its uses in agriculture and ritual, transport, and technology. We will explore water's impact on public health and the effects of water pollution on local societies. Finally, we will focus on the effects of the region's water scarcity in cross-border political conflicts.

source.text: HIST 273. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | PWAD 273 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of the Ottoman Empire, 1300-1923
courses.description: Approaches the history of the Ottoman Empire from a world historical perspective. Situates the Ottoman imperial experience in relation to Muslim, Mongolian, and Byzantine traditions. Discusses the early modern and modern transformation of the Ottoman Empire and its legacy for contemporary Eastern Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: African History to 1800
courses.description: Course explores history of the African continent from before agriculture to the era of the Transatlantic slave trade. Particular attention given to themes such as trade, religion, and politics as well as the sources and methods for knowing about the premodern African past.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Modern Middle East
courses.description: This course introduces students to the recent history of the Middle East, including a comparison of the Middle East to the United States.

source.text: HIST 276. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | ASIA 276 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Conflict over Israel/Palestine
courses.description: Explores the conflict over Palestine during the last 100 years. Surveys the development of competing nationalisms, the contest for resources and political control that led to the partition of the region, the war that established a Jewish state, and the subsequent struggles between conflicting groups for land and independence.

source.text: HIST 277. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | ASIA 277 , PWAD 277 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
courses.description: Focused on one of the most tragic and horrifying phenomena in world history, this course examines the Atlantic slave trade and its demographic, economic, political, and cultural impact on four continents over three centuries. Through interactive lectures, discussions, and a variety of written assignments, students will learn about this monumental and far-reaching system while sharpening critical thinking and communication skills. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern South Africa
courses.description: Beginning with the discovery of gold and diamonds in the mid-19th century and reaching to the present, this course considers colonialism, industrialization, social change, and political protest in South Africa, with particular attention to the rise, fall, and legacies of apartheid. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Women and Gender in Latin American History
courses.description: Examines the experiences of women and gender relations in Latin American societies from pre-Columbian times to the present, providing a new perspective on the region's historical development.

source.text: HIST 280. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | WGST 280 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Pacific War, 1937-1945: Its Causes and Legacy
courses.description: An examination of the origins of the Pacific War, the course of this bitter and momentous conflict, and its complex legacy for both Asia and the United States.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: China in the World
courses.description: This course explores the evolution of China as a geopolitical entity from global perspectives, 1350 to the present.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Chairman Mao's China in World History
courses.description: To put the recent transformation of the People's Republic of China in context, the course examines the different facets of Maoism that governed the country in its early years. It highlights Maoism as a global force that paved the way for China's re-integration into the world order. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Late Imperial China
courses.description: This course introduces undergraduates to significant themes of the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) dynasties. Topics include family, religion, art, fiscal change, trade networks, conquest, emperorship, Manchu ethnicity, the examination system and book culture, legal codes, gender, the Taiping Rebellion, and the Boxer Uprising, among others. No prior coursework required.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern Chinese History
courses.description: This survey course will introduce students to the major events, people and themes of modern Chinese history. At the end of the nineteenth century, China was an empire on the brink of collapse. Today, China is the next global superpower. What are the significant events, people and themes that impacted this major transformation? How has the trajectory of China's recent past influenced its position and challenges in the present?

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Modern Japan
courses.description: Explores Japan's history, culture, and society from the Meiji Restoration of 1868 to the present.

source.text: HIST 288. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | ASIA 288 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: America in the 1970s
courses.description: This course will explore how Americans in the 1970s responded to crises, challenges, and opportunities, and how they ultimately remade ideas of identity, citizenship, work, family, and culture.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Putting Literature and History in Dialogue
courses.description: Dialogues between historiographic and fictional treatments of important historical problems. Explores works of history and literature to determine how different genres of writing give meaning to the past. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Thinking Historically
courses.description: This class will examine the skills associated with historical thinking and the application of those skills across many contexts. The course will involve guest speakers who use historical thinking in their work and daily lives as well as assignments aimed at applying historical thinking to uses inside and outside of the classroom. The final project will involve the class curating, annotating, and sharing a collection of primary sources with a wider public. We will work together to decide upon the topic, sources, format, and audience.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The World of Catherine de'Medici: Gender, Power, and Conflict in Sixteenth-Century France
courses.description: This course uses Catherine de'Medici as a point of entry into an exploration of France in the latter half of the sixteenth century. There are three complementary lenses. The first is gender history. The second lens is power. What exactly was power and what did it mean to be powerful in Catherine's world? The third lens is violence. Why was France so unusually violent in this period? The course is deliberately structured so as to interweave these perspectives, as well as to introduce others, including the first French attempts at trans-Atlantic expansion, visual culture, and the insights of microhistory.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: How Empires Fall: Case Studies from the Past and Lessons for Today
courses.description: What are empires, and how do they fall? This course examines the collapse of the three historical empires, explores discussions of modern decolonization, and addresses the question of what empire looks like in the contemporary world.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Movies Make History: Films as Primary Sources in Europe and America
courses.description: This course explains how and why certain films helped shape the medium even as they reflected broader aspects of historical change. Beginning with the development of narrative film in 1908, the course looks at those nationally specific genres that had repercussions beyond national borders, ending in about 1968. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Medieval Spain
courses.description: This course traces Iberian history from the eleventh to fifteenth centuries, focusing specifically on two related developments: frontier conditions that accompanied the progressive conquest of Muslim al-Andalus by the northern Christian kingdoms of Castile and Aragon and the multicultural, multireligious socities that resulted. We will study social relations on the ground within and between communities of Jews, Christians, and Muslims under conditions of constant change over the course of more than four centuries.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Conquest and Colonization in the English Atlantic World
courses.description: This course explores the history of conquest and the political-military process of establishing control in the British Isles (including Ireland) and how those processes created expectations and policies as the English moved into the New World. We will examine both European precedents and colonial transformations. We will explore how European (especially English) society functioned, and how it was transformed in the New World.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Elizabeth I and her World: Gender, Power, and the Beginnings of the Global
courses.description: This class explores the world of Elizabeth I of England (1558-1603) through three complementary lenses: the queen as powerful political actor; gender; and emergent globalization. Particular attention is paid to the ways in which Elizabeth fashioned the images that she projected, and how she was perceived by others.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Princes and Reformations in Germany, 1400-1600
courses.description: Examines the major late medieval religious, social, and political developments plus the Reformation and Counter-Reformation. Topics include Luther's theology, the German Peasant's War, Jewish-Christian relations, witch-hunting, and family life. Previously offered as HIST 460.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Religion, Statecraft, and Enlightenment in Germany, 1600-1815
courses.description: Examines major political, social, and cultural developments. Topics include the growth of absolutist government, Prussia's militarism and rivalry with Austria, German Jewry, Baroque music, the Enlightenment, and the Napoleonic wars. Previously offered as HIST 461.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Renaissance and the Jews
courses.description: The Renaissance (1300-1600) is known as a time of great artistic, scientific, and political renewal. But did Jews, the only religious minority in Europe, get an opportunity to benefit from and participate in that progress? This class studies the history of the Jews at a time of great cultural change.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Old Regime France, 1661-1787
courses.description: This course focuses on the period in French history between the ascendancy of absolute monarchy in the middle of the 17th century and the collapse of absolutism at the onset of the French Revolution.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The French Revolution
courses.description: The French Revolution was a source of much that the modern world recognizes as its own: nationalism, human rights, class conflict, ideology, communism, conservatism, show trials, citizen armies, terrorism, and the concept of revolution itself. This course probes issues that underlie the continuing relevance of the French Revolution today.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Ghettos and Shtetls? Urban Life in East European Jewish History
courses.description: The migration of Jewish populations from small towns to large cities in Eastern Europe altered notions of Jewish community, space, cultures, and identities. This course will explore the roles of ghetto and shtetl in both history and memory of the Jewish past, drawing on memoirs, literature, film, and photography. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of France and Algeria
courses.description: This course covers France's conquest, rule, and loss of Algeria, and the relationship between French and Algerian people in Algeria and France from 1830 to the present. Topics such as modern French and North African history, colonialism, Islam, immigration, terror/torture, and cross-cultural exchange are all featured in this transnational course.

source.text: HIST 312. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | PWAD 312 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Women and the Law in Africa and the Middle East
courses.description: Explores women's and men's engagement with colonial and post-colonial legal systems with a focus on the 19th through 21st centuries. Topics include customary law, Islamic law, women's rights as human rights, disputation and conflict resolution. We will ask the question: "how does gender influence how women and men navigate legal systems?" Course previously offered as WMST 289.

source.text: HIST 313. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | WGST 313 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Law and Society in Latin America
courses.description: This course considers how a wide variety of groups in Latin America including indigenous people, Afro-descendant communities, women and religious minorities used the law to shape and challenge larger structures of imperial rule.

source.text: HIST 314. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST. | LTAM 314 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Nation-Building in Latin America
courses.description: This course focuses on Mexico, several Caribbean and South America countries, and the U.S. as examples of the major debates that have arisen in the past and in our own time over citizenship and the nation-state in the multi-ethnic and culturally complex societies of the Americas. It explores history and memory around issues of human rights, gender, enslavement and emancipation, Indigenous peoples, religion and secular society, territory, and the nation-state. Previously offered as HIST 529. Honors version available.

source.text: HIST 315. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST, RESEARCH.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Art, History, and the Modern Museum
courses.description: Focusing on art, history, and ethnography museums in Europe and North America, this course considers the emergence and development of museums as powerful social and cultural institutions from the mid-18th century to the 21st century. A variety of perspectives on museums showcase their connections to larger political and cultural trends.

source.text: HIST 320. | 3 Credits. | FC-AESTH or FC-PAST, RESEARCH. | ARTH 330 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Technology and American Culture
courses.description: Technology's impact on American thought and society and the response it has engendered. Topics will include the factory town, search for utopia, impact of Henry Ford, war, and depersonalization. Previously offered as HIST 625.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Food and History
courses.description: An examination of how food, its production, distribution, and consumption have shaped the history of the United States, the United Kingdom, and the world at large. The course will study how these nations and their empires have been intertwined but remained distinctive from colonial times to the present.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: History of the Computer
courses.description: This course surveys the long history of computer technology and its social, political, economic, and cultural consequences, with a particular focus on the experience of the United States.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: An Introduction to the History of Medicine
courses.description: This course underscores the ways in which Western medicine has become a global political and cultural phenomenon in history, and discusses evidence of how different social actors have parsed the distinction between sickness and health over time. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Jesus and the Jews: From the Bible to the Big Screen
courses.description: This class will study the history of the claim that the Jews are responsible for Christ's death. Students will examine the power of this idea to travel through time and space and discuss how it is portrayed differently and with different purposes throughout history. Honors version available.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Why History Matters to Public Policy
courses.description: This course explores the uses of history and historical perspectives for public policy. Students will learn how historical processes have shaped today's public policies and examine how the origins and development of a policy can inform current policy decisions. Previously offered as PLCY 231.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Identity and Community in Modern Jewish History: The Case of Durham
courses.description: This course explores diverse experiences of modernity among Jewish populations from the mid-18th century to the present under the influence of political, cultural, and socioeconomic changes. Diaries, memoirs, literature, and film challenge students to develop their own analyses while becoming familiar with arguments among scholars of Jewish life.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Love and Politics in Early India
courses.description: This course will study the social, political, and cultural history of early India, through a focus on love and desire. It will examine a range of primary sources from the period: erotic manuals, inscriptions, literature, legal and medical textbooks, art and architecture.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Rasputin's Russia: Erotic, Decadent, Revolutionary
courses.description: The turn of the 20th century was characterized by a highly stylized angst, and nowhere more so than in Russia. This course explores how the political, social, cultural, and economic transformations that vibrated throughout Russia provided a fertile context for the burst of creativity that spawned its modernist artistic movements.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Cracking India: Partition and Its Legacy in South Asia
courses.description: What happened when the British carved Pakistan out of the predominately Muslim corners of India? Readings and films focus on the causes and consequences of this event, the Partition of India. Honors version available.

source.text: HIST 335. | 3 Credits. | FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST, RESEARCH. | ASIA 331 , PWAD 331 .

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: The Mongol Empire and its Successors in Eurasia, 1100-1600
courses.description: This course is dedicated to the history of the Mongol Empire and its successor states across Eurasia between 1100-1600. Over the past generation there has been a great renaissance in the study of Mongol-ruled polities from China to Iran and beyond.
